PA3605 Cosmology: additional material for Lecture 3

Co-moving co-ordinates and the scale factor

The fact that the Universe is homogeneous and isotropic allow us to make a change in co-ordinates. Rather than using physical distances, which change with time due to the Universe’s expansion, we instead define “co-moving co-ordinates” which are independent of the expansion. As the expansion is uniform, the relationship between a physical (vector) length 𝐫⁢(t) and a co-moving length 𝐱⁢(t) can be defined as

𝐫⁢(t)=a⁢(t)⁢𝐱⁢(t) (1)

where the dimensionless number a⁢(t) is referred to as the scale factor. The Universe is homogeneous, so the scale factor is only a function of time. As the Universe expands, points (or galaxies!) remain fixed in co-moving space but change position in physical space. One can think of this as the co-ordinate system expanding with time, with the scale factor specifying the form of the expansion.

Co-ordinate and notation conventions

There are various ways to define the scale factor, and different authors use different notations. In this module I have followed the conventions used in Liddle’s textbook (An Introduction to Modern Cosmology): both physical [𝐫⁢(t)] and co-moving [𝐱⁢(t)] co-ordinates have dimensions of length, and the scale-factor a⁢(t) is therefore dimensionless. This is the most commonly-used notation in modern cosmology, but it is by no means universal. Some textbooks (notably Ryden’s Introduction to Cosmology) adopt slightly different units, which results in extra constants appearing in some of the equations, while older books often used completely different notation (e.g., dimensionless co-moving co-ordinates and a dimensional scale-factor). These changes in notation don’t affect the physics but do make some of the equations look different, so please take care when referring to material from different sources. Note also that older versions of this course did not use the same convention adopted here, so you may find inconsistencies in notation when looking at past exam papers from 2021 or earlier (most commonly R⁢(t) being used for the scale-factor).

The Friedmann equation

The Friedmann equation describes the expansion of the Universe. The relativistic version is derived from Einstein’s field equations, which relate gravity to the curvature of space-time, but we can derive the Newtonian equivalent from conservation of energy as follows.

We consider a uniform expanding medium, with mass density ρ. Because the Universe is homogeneous and isotropic, any point can be considered its centre. We consider a “test particle” with mass m (i.e., a small volume enclosing mass m) at a (physical) distance r from this central point. We can show from Gauss’ law (or Newton’s theorem) that the gravitational force on the test particle only depends on the mass at radii less than r, and the gravitational potential energy of the test particle is therefore

U=−G⁢Menc⁢mr (2)

where Menc=(4/3)⁢π⁢r3⁢ρ is the mass enclosed in a sphere of radius r. Substituting, we therefore have

U=−4⁢π⁢G⁢r2⁢ρ⁢m3 (3)

Similarly the kinetic energy of the test particle is

K=12⁢m⁢r˙2 (4)

(using dots to denote time derivatives), and the total energy is therefore

E=U+K=12⁢m⁢r˙2−4⁢π3⁢G⁢ρ⁢m⁢r2 (5)

We now introduce the scale factor by switching to co-moving co-ordinates, using Equation 1 above. Positions in co-moving co-ordinates are fixed (by definition), so 𝐱˙≡0 and

𝐫˙⁢(t)=a˙⁢(t)⁢𝐱 (6)

Substituting, we therefore find

E=12⁢m⁢a˙2⁢x2−4⁢π3⁢G⁢ρ⁢m⁢a2⁢x2 (7)

We then multiply both sides by 2/m⁢a2⁢x2 to find

2⁢Em⁢a2⁢x2=(a˙a)2−8⁢π⁢G3⁢ρ (8)

and re-arrange to find

(a˙a)2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢ρ−k⁢c2a2 (9)

where we have defined k⁢c2=−2⁢E/m⁢x2. This is the standard form of the Friedmann equation111 You may also come across the Friedmann equation written in terms of the energy density ε, rather than the mass density ρ, which introduces an additional factor of c2. In general relativity the former is often preferred, but here we will work exclusively in terms of ρ. – the most important equation in cosmology.

The first two terms in this equation are independent of x, so homogeneity requires that k is also independent of x. x is independent of time, and because energy is conserved E is also independent of time, so we see that k is simply a constant (with dimensions of length-2). We will see in due course that k is related to the geometry of the Universe, and is usually referred to as the curvature (or curvature constant)222 In this Newtonian treatment k is a constant related to the total energy of the Universe, but had we taken a general relativistic approach k would be explicitly associated with the curvature of spacetime. Here we simply assert that the two forms are equivalent, and defer the detailed proof to a higher-level course..

Units again…

Cosmologists, like particle physicists, are notoriously relaxed about units, and often use so-called “natural units” in which c=1 333 Or, even more confusingly, c=G=ℏ=1!. It’s common to see the Friedmann equation written without the c2 term, but this can be confusing as it makes the units of time and length interchangeable (and dropping the c2 also changes the dimensions of k). Liddle’s textbook does do this (see the discussion in his Section 3.5), but some others do not. In practice it rarely matters, but for clarity I will retain the factors of c2, so k will have dimensions of length-2 throughout this module.

The fluid equation

In order to solve the Friedmann equation, and describe the dynamics of the Universe, we must now consider how the density ρ evolves with time, which requires us to consider the pressure of the material p. As before, the relativistic treatment of this problem formally begins with Einstein’s field equations, but we can derive the so-called fluid equation in a Newtonian framework by starting with the first law of thermodynamics

d⁢E=T⁢d⁢S−p⁢d⁢V (10)

applied to an expanding spherical volume V with physical radius r. In comoving co-ordinates we therefore have444 Liddle does this slightly differently, defining the radius to be unity in co-moving co-ordinates, but I have opted for this treatment to keep the dimensions explicit.

V=4⁢π3⁢a3⁢x3 (11)

As the energy of the volume is given by E=Menc⁢c2, we have

E=4⁢π3⁢a3⁢x3⁢ρ⁢c2 (12)

and therefore (recalling that x˙≡0)

d⁢Ed⁢t=4⁢π⁢a2⁢x3⁢ρ⁢c2⁢a˙+4⁢π3⁢a3⁢x3⁢c2⁢ρ˙ (13)

Similarly, we have

d⁢Vd⁢t=4⁢π⁢a2⁢x3⁢a˙ (14)

If we then assume that the expansion is reversible (i.e., the change in entropy d⁢S=0), then we can substitute for d⁢E and d⁢V in Equation 10 to find

4⁢π⁢a2⁢x3⁢ρ⁢c2⁢a˙+4⁢π3⁢a3⁢x3⁢c2⁢ρ˙=−4⁢π⁢a2⁢x3⁢a˙⁢p (15)

We then divide through by 4⁢π⁢a3⁢x3⁢c2 and re-arrange to find

ρ˙+3⁢a˙a⁢(ρ+pc2)=0 (16)

The evolution of the density thus depends on both the density and pressure of the material. As we will see, the expansion of the Universe therefore depends on the equation of state of the material in question (i.e., matter, radiation, or vacuum energy).

The acceleration equation

We can combine the Friedmann and fluid equations to obtain a third equation, which describes the acceleration of the Universe (and is sometimes more useful than the other forms). We first differentiate the Friedmann equation (Equation 9 above) with respect to time, using the quotient rule d/d⁢t⁢(a˙/a)=(a¨⁢a−a˙2)/a2, to find

2⁢(a˙a)⁢a⁢a¨−a˙2a2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢ρ˙+2⁢k⁢c2a3⁢a˙ (17)

The fluid equation (Equation 16) gives us

ρ˙=−3⁢a˙a⁢(ρ+pc2) (18)

and we can substitute for ρ˙ to find

2⁢(a˙a)⁢a⁢a¨−a˙2a2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢[−3⁢a˙a⁢(ρ+pc2)]+2⁢k⁢c2a3⁢a˙ (19)

We then cancel a factor of 2⁢a˙/a everywhere, and separate the fraction on the left-hand side:

a¨a−(a˙a)2=−4⁢π⁢G⁢(ρ+pc2)+k⁢c2a2 (20)

The second term here is the left-hand side of Equation 9 (the Friedmann equation again), and if we substitute for it the curvature (k⁢c2/a2) terms cancel, leaving

a¨a=−43⁢π⁢G⁢(ρ+3⁢pc2) (21)

This equation tells us about the gravitational acceleration of the Universe: the negative sign implies that both density and pressure act to decelerate the expansion (because gravity is attractive). Note also that pressure only influences the expansion of the Universe gravitationally (through mass-energy equivalence): isotropy requires that there are no pressure gradients, and therefore no other accelerations due to pressure.
